Transcript:
[00:00] Maya (AE): okay, uh hello everyone, thanks for making time. This is the week-2 prefetch hit-rate retrospective, we'll go 30, 40 minutes max, um Ravi's going to run through the numbers so I'll hand over.
[00:14] Ravi (SE): cool, thanks Maya. Quick context — we ran the extended prefetch for the last 7 days on staging and enabled prefix-KV caching for the top 20 route keys. I have a dashboard export, I'll read the highlights.
[00:29] Laura (DatumCart): awesome, hi. Quick note — we also tightened prompt dedup logic on our side last Thursday, so some delta might be due to that.
[00:40] Ravi (SE): good call, please remind us again how you canonicalize?
[00:45] Laura: yeah, so simple steps — lowercasing, strip punctuation on product names, and short form mapping for our sku types. We also collapse user chatty preambles to a single token template, that's probably the big one.
[01:02] Diego (Product): and we shipped that change Friday morning, so full-week overlap is about 5 days.
[01:08] Ravi (SE): ok, numbers — prefix hit rate on the 20-key set moved from 18% baseline to 34% average, with spikes up to 47% on low-variance routes. KV hit (exact KV lookup) w/ longer prefetch went from 12% to 22%. So overall token reuse reduced about 11% across the pilot.
[01:35] Samir (Platform): 11% token reduction sounds good — what's the observed cost delta?
[01:40] Ravi (SE): rough estimate is ~9% cost savings on our hosted footprint, but this is noisy because of mixing of large/short prompts.
[01:50] Laura: latency? Did p95 get worse with the longer prefetch windows?
[01:55] Ravi: p50 stayed roughly flat, p95 increased by about 80ms on average during steady-state, but during bursts we observed larger jumps — up to 300ms on a couple of 95th percentile samples. Likely backpressure and contention when the prefetch pipeline warms under concurrency.
[02:18] Diego: hm that p95 jump worries product — our SLOs are tight. Is that something you can mitigate with batching or different prefetch concurrency?
[02:27] Ravi: yes, two knobs — reduce prefetch parallelism per route (we saw diminishing returns beyond 4 concurrent prefetches), and increase batching window slightly to amortize compute. There's a tradeoff: more batching reduces costs but can add latency for single requests.
[02:45] Maya (AE): also worth calling out automatic prefix eviction behavior — heavy key churn on some routes caused eviction thrash which lowered hit rate mid-week. We recommended a TTL bump on stable keys.
[02:58] Samir: eviction thrash — can you quantify?
[03:02] Ravi: on route /cart/recommend the top-10 keys had churn, effective hit dropped from 40% to 24% during the churn window. We traced to a pattern: promotional SKUs push new keys causing cache churn.
[03:18] Laura: that's on us — marketing ran flash banners, apologies. We can mark those as lower priority keys to avoid prefetching.
[03:25] Diego: question — how much of the hit rate can we get by canonicalization alone vs prefetch?
[03:31] Ravi: from a quick A/B on samples, canonicalization gave us about a 9-point bump on prefix hit when applied alone. Prefetch added another 7-12 points depending on window. So both together are multiplicative-ish.
[03:47] Laura: interesting, so we should prioritize canonicalization low-effort changes immediately.
[03:52] Maya: agreed. Action item for Laura to run two targeted canonicalization experiments — one aggressive and one conservative — capture hit delta and sample prompts.
[04:02] (Laura: noted)
[04:06] Samir: on prefetch sizing — what's the staging config you ran?
[04:09] Ravi: we used prefetch depth 6, concurrency 3, TTL 30m for those top keys. On recommendation we'll try depth 8 with concurrency 2 and a TTL bump to 60m to reduce churn.
[04:23] Diego: how about memory pressure? increasing depth hurts memory on the node?
[04:27] Ravi: slight increase, but within our staging limits. For dedicated capacity we'd have headroom; on shared hosting it's tighter.
[04:34] Maya: note — customer said they want to test a dedicated run for 30 minutes under traffic to validate p95 and capacity; we'll schedule that if numbers hold.
[04:43] Ravi: also noticed some mis-attribution in the logs — KV lookups were sometimes logged as misses due to tokenization differences. We recommended normalizing token boundaries between prefixing and model tokenizers.
[04:56] Laura: yes, we saw odd mismatches. Our tokenizer on the client side is slightly different than the runtime tokenizer, so canonicalization helps but we may also need a shared tokenization shim.
[05:09] Maya: recommended short-term: canonicalization + TTL bump + concurrency tweak. Medium-term: shared tokenization shim and a small dedicated stress test.
[05:20] Diego: ok. One more — can you send the raw CSV of per-route hit rates? We want to feed into our internal dashboards.
[05:26] Maya: yes, I'll export and send.
[05:28] (short pause, typing noises)
[05:40] Ravi: quick callout on batching: our optimizer recommends a dynamic batch size up to 8 for low-latency routes with token lengths under 256; for long-requests we keep batch=1 to avoid tail latency. We can expose that as an auto-policy.
[05:58] Samir: would dynamic batching be safe with our traffic pattern? We have unpredictable spikes.
[06:03] Ravi: with the right backpressure and queue time SLOs it can be safe; we'd recommend a conservative initial policy with a max queue delay of 25ms.
[06:12] Laura: on the canonicalization experiments — what's a good sample size? We can run A/B on 10k requests each?
[06:18] Ravi: 10k should be fine for a signal. Aim to run during both peak and off-peak to capture churn effects.
[06:25] Diego: tooling question — can Redwood provide the hit-rate export per hour granularity?
[06:29] Maya: yes, we'll include hourly buckets and also a filtered export for the top 50 keys.
[06:34] (typing)
[06:46] Laura: curious — are there any gotchas we should watch for when we bump TTL to 60m? We don't want stale results for some personalization keys.
[06:55] Ravi: good point — TTL increase only recommended for stable keys i.e., global recommendations, not per-user personalization. We'll annotate keys before applying.
[07:07] Diego: ok, walkthrough of next-phase schedule?
[07:10] Maya: proposed plan in bullets: 1) Laura runs canonicalization A/B and shares samples by 7/16; 2) Redwood exports week-2 CSV by 7/11; 3) Ravi sets up staging run with depth 8/concurrency 2 and collects p50/p95 by 7/14; 4) after verifying numbers, schedule 30m dedicated stress test for week of 7/21.
[07:31] Samir: approved. Please include expected cost delta for dedicated run so finance can pre-approve.
[07:37] Maya: will include cost estimate.
[07:39] Laura: two quick questions — the tokenizer shim, is that heavy to stand up?
[07:44] Ravi: relatively light — we've shipped it as a small library before; the main cost is validating parity across edge cases. We can prototype in a day or two.
[07:53] Diego: are there any competitors who do autosuggest prefetching more aggressively?
[07:58] Maya: a few players (Anthropic, OpenAI) have higher-level managed features, but our differentiation is tuning controls + telemetry for production economics.
[08:10] (brief crosstalk about scheduling)
[08:18] Maya: ok, recap of action items: (1) Maya send CSV + notes (2) Ravi run the depth-8 staging run and share p50/p95 and traces (3) Laura run canonicalization A/B and share sample prompts + hit deltas. We also agreed to schedule the dedicated stress test pending those results.
[08:40] Diego: looks good. Any blockers from Redwood?
[08:44] Ravi: none, just need access to the canonicalization test group traffic and permission to tag keys for TTL bump.
[08:52] Laura: granted. We'll share a list of lower-priority keys to exclude from prefetch as well.
[08:58] Maya: perfect. I'll follow up after call with the dashboard export and a short doc with recommended staging config changes.
[09:07] (meeting wraps, informal chatter)

End of transcript.
